story.headline: Texas steamrolls Clemson, 49-17
body: Texas dominated from start to finish in a 49-17 rout over Clemson in Week 11 PCFL action, with Arch Manning earning Player of the Game honors after going for 29 of 47 for 409 yards and 5 TDs.
The Longhorns outgained Clemson 576–278 in total offense, including 171 yards on the ground. Clemson kept fighting, managing 278 total yards on the night.
Up next, Texas hosts Penn State in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: Manning's arm too much for Clemson in dominant 49-17 Texas rout
body: Arch Manning put on a clinic in the second half, turning what looked like a competitive matchup into a complete dismantling. The Texas quarterback finished 29 of 47 for 409 yards and five touchdowns, finding soft spots in Clemson's coverage all afternoon. What made the performance remarkable wasn't just volume—it was efficiency. Manning rarely held the ball longer than needed and made clean decisions under pressure, letting his receivers settle into routes rather than forcing balls into tight windows.

Texas's ground game gave Manning time to operate. Running back Wisner carried the load with 101 yards on nine carries, including two short-yardage scores that took pressure off the passing attack. That balance—101 rushing yards paired with 405 passing—gave the Clemson defense no rhythm to find. Meanwhile, Clemson's quarterback Cortez managed only 247 yards and struggled with timing throughout the day. The Tigers were held to just 49 rushing yards, a sign that their offensive line couldn't establish any foundation.

Clemson's defense couldn't generate sustained pressure despite three opportunities from turnovers. Defensive end Carter logged six tackles and a sack, staying active even as his teammates fell out of sync. But one player's effort wasn't enough against a Texas team that controlled line of scrimmage on both sides. The 32-point margin reflects a complete performance from Texas—field position, execution, and limiting mistakes all aligned at once.
aiStory.turningPoint: Late in the second quarter, Manning connected with Worthy for a 101-yard reception that broke the game open and forced Clemson into a 32-7 hole entering halftime, essentially deciding the outcome.

unsungHero.name: Biles
unsungHero.why: While Manning rightfully earned Player of the Game honors, Biles's two sacks and three tackles set the tone for Texas's defensive dominance, keeping Clemson's offense off-balance and preventing any rhythm-building drives that might have kept the score respectable.

story.headline: Arkansas pulls away from Michigan, 34-16
body: Arkansas asserted control when it mattered in a 34-16 win over Michigan in Week 11 PCFL action, with K.J. Jackson earning Player of the Game honors after going for 20 of 39 for 313 yards and 2 TDs.
The Razorbacks outgained Michigan 413–385 in total offense, including 107 yards on the ground. Michigan kept fighting, managing 385 total yards on the night.
Up next, Arkansas hosts Ohio State in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: Arkansas defense suffocates Michigan in road win despite turnover trouble
body: Arkansas walked out of Ann Arbor with a 34-16 victory that looked more dominant than the yardage totals suggest. K.J. Jackson orchestrated an efficient passing attack that leaned on vertical shots downfield, completing 20 of 39 attempts for 313 yards and two touchdowns. The difference wasn't volume—Michigan's Browne actually threw for 344 yards—but rather timing and field position. Arkansas methodically converted Michigan mistakes into points, and when the Razorbacks needed a stop, their defense delivered.

The turning point arrived in the third quarter when Arkansas's defensive line, anchored by Worth Jr's relentless pursuit, forced Michigan into consecutive negative plays. Worth Jr's two sacks dismantled drive momentum at critical junctures, and while the box score may not fully capture it, Michigan's run game—bottled up at 83 yards—never found rhythm. Browne was forced into uncomfortable situations, checking down more often than attacking vertically. Meanwhile, Parker's vertical catches for Arkansas, particularly his 121-yard day on six receptions including a touchdown, punished Michigan's secondary when it sat too shallow.

Arkansas surrendered two fumbles yet still dictated the tempo and outcome. The coaching room's decision to commit to light box coverage, trusting the pass rush to generate pressure, proved shrewd against Michigan's run-first mentality. Burkett's 10 carries netted only 45 yards—a damning indictment of how thoroughly the Razorback front seven took that phase away. When Michigan tried to establish anything sustained, Arkansas reset and reset again.
aiStory.turningPoint: Worth Jr's two sacks in the third quarter collapsed Michigan's offensive rhythm and shifted field position decisively in Arkansas's favor, turning a close game into a runaway.

unsungHero.name: Worth Jr
unsungHero.why: Jackson earned Player of the Game, but Worth Jr's two sacks and relentless edge pressure were the foundational reason Michigan never sustained drives or built scoring momentum—defensive dominance doesn't always get headlines.

story.headline: Boston College takes control late, tops Georgia 37-21
body: Boston College asserted control when it mattered in a 37-21 win over Georgia in Week 11 PCFL action, with Bo MacCormick earning Player of the Game honors after going for 50 rushing yards and 2 rushing TDs.
The Eagles were outgained by Georgia 399–382 in total offense, including 168 yards on the ground. Georgia kept fighting, managing 399 total yards on the night.
Up next, Boston College travels to face Oklahoma in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: Boston College ground game overwhelms Georgia in defensive showcase
body: Boston College's ground attack proved decisive on Saturday, with the Eagles grinding out 168 rushing yards to control the line of scrimmage and dictate pace. While Georgia's passing game stayed busy through the air—Giles connecting on 22 completions for 304 yards and three scores—the Eagles' defense bent without breaking, forcing a crucial turnover that shifted momentum late. Bo MacCormick's 10-carry performance anchored a complementary football approach that kept Georgia's pass-heavy offense on its heels for stretches.

The turning point came when Georgia's offense stalled in the fourth quarter after a fumble deep in Boston College territory. That turnover, coupled with the Eagles' methodical clock management through their rushing attack, essentially sealed the game. Georgia managed 285 passing yards but couldn't generate enough chunk plays on the ground to balance the attack. Leavitt's 20-for-28 efficiency and a touchdown pass suggested Boston College's offense merely needed to stay in rhythm rather than chase Georgia through a shootout.

Georgia's defensive unit, led by Wilson's sack, couldn't manufacture consistent stops when it mattered most. Boston College's ability to sustain drives through power running kept Georgia's pass rush from generating critical third-down situations. The Eagles outgained Georgia in total yards by a thin margin, yet controlled the game's complexion through field position and eliminating mistakes. This was a lesson in how complementary football—rush yards, turnover avoidance, and defensive discipline—can neutralize superior passing volume.
aiStory.turningPoint: Georgia's late-game fumble inside Boston College territory halted any momentum swing and allowed the Eagles to milk clock with their ground game in the final minutes.

unsungHero.name: Davis
unsungHero.why: Davis led all defenders with six tackles and a sack, quietly anchoring the Eagles' pass rush without the fanfare of the player-of-the-game honor.

story.headline: LSU pulls away from Tennessee, 17-7
body: LSU asserted control when it mattered in a 17-7 win over Tennessee in Week 11 PCFL action, with Tim Ferguson earning Player of the Game honors after going for 50 rushing yards and 2 rushing TDs.
The Tigers outgained Tennessee 329–200 in total offense, including 157 yards on the ground. Tennessee kept fighting, managing 200 total yards on the night.
Up next, LSU hosts USC in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: LSU's Ground Game Grinds Down Tennessee in Defensive Struggle
body: LSU's offense never sparkled on Saturday, but it didn't need to. Tim Ferguson carved out 50 yards on 12 carries and punched in two touchdowns, anchoring a dominant ground attack that controlled the line of scrimmage and the clock. Tennessee's defense had no answer for the relentless run game, and with Nussmeier managing rather than forcing the issue through the air, LSU's coaching room kept the chains moving and the scoreboard ticking in their favor.

The numbers tell the story of a program that executed its identity. LSU out-gained Tennessee 329 to 200 and held the ball long enough to wear down a Volunteer defense that couldn't generate consistent stops. Tennessee's Bishop ran hard for 91 yards and found the end zone once, but it amounted to damage control. MacIntyre and the passing game never found rhythm, and the offense sputtered whenever it tried to keep pace.

Where LSU's defense truly separated itself was in protecting the football. A single fumble lost versus Tennessee's unforced turnover proved decisive in a game decided by 10 points. Ross sacked Nussmeier twice for Tennessee and showed up when he could, but his effort came too late in a contest where field position and time of possession already favored the visiting team.
aiStory.turningPoint: Ferguson's second touchdown run late in the third quarter effectively put the game out of reach, as Tennessee's offense had shown no ability to match LSU's sustained drives.

unsungHero.name: Stafford
unsungHero.why: His five tackles and sack went largely unheralded because Ferguson's two touchdown runs captured all the attention, but Stafford's work in containing Tennessee's ground game and disrupting MacIntyre's timing was foundational to the shutout performance in the second half.

story.headline: Instant classic: Penn State edges Miami, 20-17
body: Penn State found just enough in a 20-17 thriller over Miami in Week 11 PCFL action, with Mallik Myers earning Player of the Game honors after going for 26 of 48 for 341 yards and 1 TD.
The Nittany Lions outgained Miami 461–356 in total offense, including 124 yards on the ground. Miami kept fighting, managing 356 total yards on the night.
Up next, Penn State travels to face Texas in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: Myers steadies Penn State in tight defensive grind over Miami
body: Penn State's offense found just enough rhythm to outlast Miami in a game where both defenses made their presence felt throughout. Mallik Myers completed 26 of 48 passes for 341 yards and a touchdown, proving efficient enough to navigate a Miami secondary that kept receivers from breaking free downfield. The real separation came on the ground, where Penn State's rushing attack — led by Jenkins and his one-yard touchdown plunge — generated 124 yards compared to Miami's anemic 54, a gap that proved decisive in a three-point finish.

Miami's passing game showed moments of competence through the work of receiver Jackson, who hauled in nine catches for 86 yards and provided a reliable safety valve for quarterback Mertz. Yet Mertz managed just 180 yards on 18 completions, a sign that Penn State's defensive front disrupted timing and rhythm in ways the box score alone doesn't capture. The Hurricanes' inability to establish anything resembling a ground game left them one-dimensional and predictable, a vulnerability Penn State's defense exploited without generating spectacular splash plays.

Neither team committed a turnover, which meant this came down to execution and field position. Penn State's 461 total yards versus Miami's 356 reflected a team that simply moved the ball with greater consistency. The three-point margin understates Penn State's control of this matchup — they dictated pace, leaned on the run, and made Myers a complementary piece rather than a franchise savior. Miami will rue opportunities left on the field, but the truth is Penn State's staff managed the game better when it mattered most.
aiStory.turningPoint: Jenkins' touchdown run in the second half gave Penn State a two-score lead that Miami never recovered from, forcing the Hurricanes into a pass-first approach that negated their limited run game.

unsungHero.name: Taylor
unsungHero.why: Four catches for 80 yards kept chains moving and provided Myers with reliable targets on third downs, but his work went unheralded while Myers claimed all the spotlight despite an inconsistent completion percentage.

story.headline: Ohio State makes a statement in 45-17 rout of Oklahoma
body: Ohio State dominated from start to finish in a 45-17 rout over Oklahoma in Week 11 PCFL action, with Bo Jackson earning Player of the Game honors.
The Buckeyes outgained Oklahoma 367–264 in total offense, including 170 yards on the ground. Oklahoma kept fighting, managing 264 total yards on the night.
Up next, Ohio State travels to face Arkansas in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: Ohio State's ground game overwhelms Oklahoma in dominant Week 11 statement
body: Ohio State dismantled Oklahoma 45-17 on Saturday, a performance that revealed the gap between a team executing its identity and one searching for answers. The Buckeyes' rushing attack, led by the announced Player of the Game Bo Jackson, churned out 170 yards and set the tone from the opening drive. That early commitment to the run game opened sight lines for QB Sayin, who completed 19 of 31 passes for 207 yards and three touchdowns without needing to air it out constantly. When a team can move the ball on the ground with that kind of authority, the passing game becomes a precision instrument rather than a desperate one.

Oklahoma's defense, anchored by Williams's eight tackles, simply could not establish a line of scrimmage. The Sooners' offense kept pace for stretches, with QB Glass throwing for 179 yards and two scores on efficient 20-for-27 accuracy, but the inability to establish any running identity—just 99 rushing yards on the day—forced Glass into predictable passing situations. Wilcots managed only 53 yards on six carries, a stat line that tells the story of an offensive line getting pushed around. Without a credible ground threat, Oklahoma became one-dimensional, and Ohio State's defense tightened its coverage accordingly.

The turnover margin told another tale. Ohio State coughed it up three times but forced two fumbles from Oklahoma and held the Sooners to one. In a game this lopsided, though, field position and rhythm mattered more than individual mistakes. Ohio State's staff kept Oklahoma constantly backpedaling, and that relentless pace prevented any momentum shift. This wasn't a close contest with a dramatic swing—it was a methodical dismantling where one team's game plan worked and the other's didn't.
aiStory.turningPoint: Ohio State's third offensive drive, a sustained ground-based march that resulted in a touchdown, essentially put the game out of reach by establishing that Oklahoma could not match the Buckeyes' physical identity at the line of scrimmage.

unsungHero.name: Roker
unsungHero.why: Seven tackles and zero sacks might seem pedestrian, but Roker's consistent presence in the middle of the field disrupted Oklahoma's ability to find rhythm. He didn't rack up the highlight plays, but his work set the foundation for an overwhelmingly successful defensive gameplan that allowed the offense to control tempo.

story.headline: UCLA takes control late, tops Oregon 20-10
body: UCLA asserted control when it mattered in a 20-10 win over Oregon in Week 11 PCFL action, with Nico Iamaleava earning Player of the Game honors after going for 19 of 29 for 270 yards and 1 TD.
The Bruins outgained Oregon 392–263 in total offense, including 139 yards on the ground. Oregon kept fighting, managing 263 total yards on the night.
Up next, UCLA hosts Georgia in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: UCLA's passing game breaks Oregon's defensive will in road victory
body: UCLA's offense operated with surgical precision in the second half, exploiting Oregon's depleted secondary with a balanced attack that Oregon's defensive front simply could not disrupt. The Bruins moved the ball 392 yards with minimal resistance, and while the final margin of ten points suggests a competitive game, the gap in execution was wider than the scoreboard indicated. Nico Iamaleava threaded passes into tight windows all afternoon, completing 19 of 29 attempts for 270 yards and a touchdown, and his poise under pressure—Oregon never generated consistent heat—allowed UCLA's receivers to work in rhythm downfield.

Oregon's offensive identity crumbled against UCLA's pass rush. Thomas finished 11 of 27 for just 121 yards, a cautionary tale of what happens when a quarterback must hold the ball longer while receivers struggle to separate. Hughes provided the only genuine spark, grinding out 77 yards on 12 carries and punching in a touchdown, but one dimension could not sustain an entire offense. The Ducks' coaching staff will recognize that settling into a run-heavy approach after falling behind proved too passive; UCLA's defense tightened coverage and dared Thomas to beat them downfield, and he could not meet the challenge.

What began as a grinding, field-position game tilted decisively toward UCLA when the Bruins' secondary and pass rush synchronized in the third quarter, forcing Oregon into three straight three-and-outs. Those possessions represented the turning point—momentum never returned to Eugene. UCLA's defense, anchored by Pleasant's four tackles and a sack, suffocated Oregon's rhythm and allowed the Bruins' offense to dictate tempo. This was a game decided not by explosive plays but by control, and UCLA's coaching room imposed it from start to finish.
aiStory.turningPoint: Oregon's three consecutive three-and-outs in the third quarter, triggered by UCLA's coordinated pass rush and coverage adjustments, allowed the Bruins to build an insurmountable lead while the Ducks' offense never found rhythm.

unsungHero.name: Pleasant
unsungHero.why: Four tackles and a sack from the defensive line may not generate the same attention as Iamaleava's passing performance, but shutting down Thomas's pocket and forcing Oregon into hurried decisions was every bit as crucial to the outcome as any touchdown pass.

story.headline: Washington takes control late, tops Colorado 42-24
body: Washington asserted control when it mattered in a 42-24 win over Colorado in Week 11 PCFL action, with Jordan Washington earning Player of the Game honors after going for 59 rushing yards and 2 rushing TDs.
The Huskies outgained Colorado 474–330 in total offense, including 143 yards on the ground. Colorado kept fighting, managing 330 total yards on the night.
Up next, Washington travels to face Tennessee in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: Washington's Ground Game Overwhelms Colorado in Decisive Week 11 Rout
body: Washington dismantled Colorado 42-24 on Saturday, a victory that hinged entirely on establishing dominance in the trenches. The Huskies' offense controlled the line of scrimmage throughout, accumulating 474 total yards and forcing Colorado into a reactive posture from the opening drive. Though the score suggests a blowout, the game's true nature was one of steady, methodical suffocation rather than explosive fireworks.

Jordan Washington proved why he deserved Player of the Game honors, scoring twice on just 11 carries for 59 yards and essentially shortening the field with every touch. The offensive line's work created the space; Washington simply finished what was in front of him. Meanwhile, Williams Jr. managed the game with precision, completing 29 of 41 passes for 331 yards and a touchdown while keeping turnovers to a minimum. The Huskies' defense wasn't flashy either—Day's six tackles led a unit that didn't record a sack—but the red-shirted Colorado offense never found rhythm or breathing room.

Colorado's Anderson was prolific in defeat, throwing for 283 yards and three touchdowns despite the lopsided scoreline. Mecum's four receptions for 66 yards and a touchdown showed the Buffaloes possessed individual talent. But talent alone cannot overcome structural disadvantage. Washington's 143 rushing yards to Colorado's 58 tells the real story of the afternoon: a team that won by controlling what happens at the snap.
aiStory.turningPoint: Washington established a 21-10 halftime lead by imposing its ground game early, forcing Colorado into second-half desperation while the Huskies' defense remained stingy enough to prevent a meaningful rally.

unsungHero.name: Williams Jr.
unsungHero.why: His 29-of-41 efficiency and turnover management were the foundation of Washington's methodical control, yet the Player of the Game went to the running back in an offensive performance defined by balance and execution rather than volume.

story.headline: Notre Dame takes control late, tops USC 28-16
body: Notre Dame asserted control when it mattered in a 28-16 win over USC in Week 11 PCFL action, with CJ Carr earning Player of the Game honors after going for 23 of 39 for 286 yards and 4 TDs.
The Fighting Irish outgained USC 348–331 in total offense, including 65 yards on the ground. USC kept fighting, managing 331 total yards on the night.
Up next, Notre Dame travels to face Clemson in Week 12.

aiStory.headline: Carr's four touchdowns lift Notre Dame past USC in defensive struggle
body: Notre Dame's offense found its rhythm when it mattered most, with quarterback CJ Carr orchestrating a methodical performance that overwhelmed USC despite the Trojans keeping pace statistically. Carr's four touchdown passes on 23 completions gave the visiting defense room to operate, and they did, with linebacker Lucas recording 15 tackles to set the tone up front. The numbers tell a story of efficiency meeting execution: Notre Dame's passing attack netted 283 yards while USC generated 277, yet the gap in the final score reflected something deeper than raw yardage.

The turning point arrived in USC's inability to capitalize on possessions that should have yielded more. Moss completed 23 of 40 passes and found Ford downfield for 98 receiving yards, but the Trojans managed only 16 points from their efforts. A fumble late in the game crystallized the difference—possession after possession, Notre Dame's offense converted while USC's stalled. The defensive unit for Notre Dame, anchored by Lucas's workmanlike performance, never allowed the Trojans to string together the kind of drive that would break the game open.

This was a game decided not by highlight reel plays but by the accumulation of small advantages. Carr and Notre Dame's coaching room found a formula: get the ball to Southall on the perimeter where he could operate, attack vertically with confidence, and let the defense manage possessions. USC had moments—Ford's 98 yards showed the explosive potential was there—but consistency eluded them when it counted. Notre Dame leaves with a decisive 12-point victory that feels more convincing than the total yards suggest.
aiStory.turningPoint: USC's fumble in the fourth quarter came at a moment when the Trojans were within striking distance, and Notre Dame's offense responded with a scoring drive that essentially sealed the game.

unsungHero.name: Shaw
unsungHero.why: The defensive end compiled five tackles in a losing effort and was one of few bright spots on a unit that couldn't consistently pressure Carr, yet his work often went unnoticed amid the offensive struggles.

weeklyWrap.headline: Texas dominates; Boston College crashes the party at the top
weeklyWrap.subhead: Week 11 saw the frontrunners flex their muscle while an unexpected challenger upended the power poll.
weeklyWrap.lead: Texas dismantled Clemson with a 49-17 blowout that announced their championship credentials without equivocation. But the real shock came from Boston College, whose 37-21 upset of Georgia—a team ranked ahead of them—signals that the top five may be far more fractured than the polls suggest.

segments.title: Texas sends a championship-caliber message
segments.body: The 32-point margin against Clemson wasn't just a win; it was a statement of intent from the top-ranked team. Texas controlled pace, dictated line of scrimmage dominance, and converted opportunities without a hint of hesitation. This is the kind of performance that shapes perception heading into the final stretch.

segments.title: Boston College topples Georgia in shock upset
segments.body: Georgia entered as the fifth-ranked team. Boston College left as proof that the playoff picture is wide open. The 37-21 outcome represents not merely an upset but a credential-builder for a program that now sits fourth in the power poll. This wasn't a fluke margin—it was a complete, convincing reversal.

segments.title: Ohio State reasserts Big Ten dominance ruthlessly
segments.body: A 45-17 dismantling of Oklahoma gave Ohio State a signature non-conference statement. The margin suggests a team firing on all cylinders when it matters most, and the Big Ten's depth looks increasingly formidable as the season enters its final act.

segments.title: Tennessee's defense strangles LSU to hold firm
segments.body: A 17-7 win over LSU isn't flashy, but Tennessee's defensive effort was suffocating. The second-ranked team held the Tigers to seven points, a performance that underscores why their ranking isn't built on smoke. Defense wins close games, and Tennessee's coaching room proved that principle is alive and well.

segments.title: Arkansas climbs over Michigan on road strength
segments.body: Arkansas's 34-16 road win over Michigan consolidates their position as a legitimate title contender at third in the power poll. The margin of victory and the environment suggest a team hitting stride precisely when the stakes rise highest.

weeklyWrap.closer: Next week's matchups will clarify whether Boston College's upset signals a genuine challenger or a one-week aberration in an increasingly volatile playoff chase.
